All mobile phones emit sine waves which are also called as constant waves.
Whereas the human body, the heart, the brain, they emit and absorb random waves.
Hence, the material used inside the Envirochip converts a constant wave into a random wave.
Mobile phones emit radiations or waves in megahertz range.
Whereas the material used inside the Envirochip emits waveforms in terahertz which is nine times higher than the megahertz waveform.
The terahertz waves from the Envirochip superimpose the lower wavelength megahertz waves of the mobile phone.
And hence, the resultant output wave is a random terahertz wave emitting out of the mobile phone.
That's the technology behind the Envirochip.

Slow growth.

Most people assume driving into water is rare,

But the truth is, 10% of all drowning deaths happen inside a vehicle.
It does not matter if you are a good driver.
It does not matter if you have been on the road for years without an accident.

A sudden mechanical failure.

Thick fog hiding a sharp turn.
It happens faster than you think.
And when it does, there's no time to figure things out.
The biggest danger in a car submersion is the crushing force of water pressure trapping you inside.
As water rises around your car, it pushes against the doors and windows with immense force, making escape almost impossible.
According to Pascal's law, force equals pressure times area.
The deeper your car sinks, the more force is applied to the doors and windows.
At just three feet underwater, the pressure against your door is equivalent to the weight of a small car pressing against it, making it nearly impossible to open.
Also, water can cause short circuits in the electrical system.
So there is a high chance that electronic windows will become unusable, which can happen quickly after submersion.
One common misconception is that you should wait for your vehicle to fill with water so the pressure equalizes, making it easier to open the door.
While technically true, experts warn this is a deadly mistake.
Your car can flip, visibility drops to zero, and panic sets in.
By the time it is full of water, it is too late.
You must escape immediately.

By the time you wrestle with a headrest, your chance of survival is gone.

back toward your heart. To do that, those veins use tiny one-way valves. They open to push blood
up, and they close to stop it from flowing back down. Varicose veins happen when those valves
get weak. Blood starts pooling, pressure builds, and the veins stretch out, which is why they look
twisted, raised, or rope-like. Spider veins are similar, just smaller. Think of them as tiny,
surface-level capillaries that become visible when they're under stress. They don't bulge like
varicose veins, but they can still burn, itch, or feel irritated. So why does this happen more as you
age? As you get older, a few things naturally change. The valves in your veins weaken. The
vein walls lose elasticity. Nighttime circulation naturally slows down, and swelling in the ankles
